sources.news_title: Anthropic to shift some shares into new ‘public good’ fund
sources.text:
Anthropic to shift some shares into new ‘public good’ fund
This could allow the company to use some of the money to address ‘labour market impacts’
ANTHROPIC said it plans to put 5 per cent of its shares into a new so-called public benefit fund that allows it to make donations that can address “the public good”, including mitigating artificial intelligence’s impact on the job market.
The announcement comes as the fast-growing AI startup prepares for an initial public offering expected to be one of the biggest ever.
At the same time, Anthropic is seeking to address rising concerns about AI safety and its potential unintended impact – from hacking to mass job losses – as companies move to adopt AI agents that can supplant human labour.
The new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund could allow the company to pursue its mission “in new ways”, such as using some of the money to address “labour market impacts”, according to the statement.
Warnings about catastrophic AI scenarios that critics say could put humanity at risk have focused attention on AI safety in recent weeks, including at top political levels.
US President Donald Trump hosted Silicon Valley leaders, including Anthropic chief executive officer Dario Amodei, at the White House in September.
With Trump rejecting the idea of new federal regulations, he and the executives agreed on a framework for AI firms to have outside auditors assess safety risks of AI models and put stronger internal controls in place.
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude large language model, may start formally marketing its IPO as soon as the week of Nov 9, which would put it on track to begin trading before the US Thanksgiving holiday, people familiar with the matter said in early October.
Anthropic said the new fund will be, subject to approval, a wholly owned LLC – rather than a non-profit – and will grow as the company grows.
None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving in the US or abroad, according to the statement.
Public benefit funds are a new type of “impact” investment fund designed to go beyond the goal of financial returns to also make a positive social or environmental impact.
“Subject to stockholder approval, 5 per cent of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2 per cent added at the board’s discretion for every 50 per cent increase in the company’s value above a set baseline,” the company said.
Anthropic recently presented its own draft bill to US lawmakers for how to regulate AI safety and security, suggesting the government could block the release of an AI model if it could risk killing or injuring more than 50 people or causing more than US$1 billion in damages.
Among those warning about AI risks are International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva, who said the technology could deliver “a slow-moving tsunami” that hollows out the low-paying job market.
Anthropic has spent much of the year in a fight with the US government that has cast a spotlight on its broader national impacts after it was labelled a supply chain risk for attempting to limit some Pentagon and other potential uses of its technology, despite previously offering its AI to develop autonomous drone technology and for other classified uses to assist military combat.
Tensions between the White House and the company have eased in recent weeks. BLOOMBERG

sources.news_title: Anthropic says it’s committing 5% of its shares to a ‘public benefit fund’
sources.text:
Anthropic announced today that it’s creating a “public benefit fund” that will give the company “increased flexibility and scale” to support projects for societal good.
Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund — structured as a wholly-owned entity within the company — with the option to contribute an additional 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s value. And it offered some broad-strokes ideas for how this money might actually be used, such as “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.”
There’s also the impact that AI might have on the job market, which Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study. But the company said, “Given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”
Anthropic’s announcement comes as the AI industry faces increasingly negative public sentiment, which CEO Dario Amodei has described as “fundamentally a crisis of trust.”
If you’re wondering who will actually decide which public benefits are worth funding, Anthropic said it will share more information about structure and governance in the coming months.

sources.news_title: Anthropic to commit 5% stake to new public benefit fund
Anthropic commits billions to a 'public benefit fund'
sources.text:
Anthropic said on Sunday that it would set aside large portions of its wealth to support initiatives it believes are in the public interest.
In a blog post, the AI colossus said it aims to establish a separate LLC that would use Anthropic shares to make donations to nonprofits or "direct distributions to specific populations."
The new LLC, called the "Anthropic Public Benefit Fund," would receive larger stakes as the company grows. The company said an initial funding round of 5% of Anthropic's shares is still subject to stockholder approval.
"The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways," the company said.
A 5% stake in Anthropic is worth about $48 billion, according to the company's most recent valuation in May.
In 2025, rival frontier AI company OpenAI established a similar nonprofit foundation with a multibillion-dollar stake in the company to fund public-benefit initiatives.

Anthropic says it will commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with additional equity tied to future value growth, subject to approval.
Anthropic said on Sunday that it will commit a portion of its shares to a new Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, describing the structure as one that would increase the stake as the company grows. The announcement matters because it frames a larger share of the company’s equity as dedicated to public benefit rather than traditional ownership or compensation use.
What Anthropic said
In its Oct. 18, 2026 statement, Anthropic said that, subject to stockholder approval, 5% of its shares will be committed immediately, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in company value above a set baseline. The company said the fund will be established as a wholly owned LLC, rather than a 501(c)(3) or similar charity, to allow flexibility between different forms of giving.
Anthropic said the fund could support large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations. As one example, the company pointed to labor-market impacts from AI, saying it has already committed $200 million to study and address that issue but that faster AI progress may require broader approaches.
Governance and context
The company said none of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the U.S. or abroad. It also said the structure builds on earlier commitments from its co-founders and employees, including a pledge by the co-founders to donate 80% of their equity holdings and an employee equity donation match program that Anthropic said covers approximately half of its workforce.
Anthropic said that, when combined with the new commitment, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that may be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones. The company said it will provide more details on the fund’s structure, governance and valuation milestones in the coming months, alongside a public benefit report on progress against its mission.
Background material supplied with the announcement notes that Anthropic is a Delaware public benefit corporation and distinguishes the company’s Long-Term Benefit Trust, which holds exclusive Class T shares for governance oversight, from the newly announced fund. That background also notes that Anthropic’s company page, as reviewed on Oct. 18, 2026, lists Neil Buddy Shah, Richard Fontaine and Ben Bernanke as trustees.
Recent related company updates included an agenda for the Economic Futures Research Fund on July 22, 2026, and the appointment of Ben Bernanke to Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust on July 9, 2026.

sources.news_title: Anthropic sets out equity commitment for public benefit fund
Anthropic ties its giving to its equity, from founder pledges to $200 million research funds
sources.text:
Anthropic official brand assets (anthropic.com)
Anthropic ties its giving to its equity, from founder pledges to $200 million research funds
The AI company's founders, employees, and corporate arm are all making charitable commitments as a potential IPO comes into view
Most companies preparing for a public listing talk about growth, margins, and market share. Anthropic is also talking about giving its stock away.
A post on X said the AI firm pledged about 20% of its shares to a public benefit fund meant to support research, gifts, and distributions. The commitments laid out in the research findings look somewhat different. They center on personal pledges from the founders, an employee stock-matching program, and two separate $200 million research commitments.
Where the money is going
All seven of Anthropic’s co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei, pledged to donate 80% of their personal equity to charity, according to the IPO prospectus.
Anthropic runs a charitable stock-matching program, and it has turned out to be expensive on paper. Between October 2025 and March 2026, the program generated over $660 million in non-cash expenses. The research findings put the total corporate contribution for 2025 at $540 million.
For the non-accountants: a non-cash expense means the company is not wiring dollars out of its bank account. It is handing over equity. That still has a cost, because new shares dilute everyone else who owns a piece of the company.
On the institutional side, Anthropic has made two headline research commitments:
AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing.
Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
- Economic Futures Research Fund: $200 million to study how AI affects labor and the broader economy, announced in July 2026.
- Gates Foundation partnership: $200 million over four years focused on AI applications in health and education, announced in May 2026.
The company has also signaled additional community-focused initiatives tied to its data centers. The research findings say those could amount to billions.
Why a public benefit corporation does this
Anthropic is organized as a Delaware public benefit corporation, or PBC. A standard company answers mainly to shareholders. A PBC is legally allowed, and expected, to weigh a stated public mission alongside profit.
Anthropic’s stated mission is to develop AI responsibly for the benefit of humanity. Its governance structure is designed to keep that goal in place and to insulate the company from some of the pressure that public markets tend to apply.
What this means for Anthropic and its future shareholders
The founders’ 80% pledge involves their personal holdings, not new shares from the company. Over time, a meaningful slice of founder equity could end up with charitable entities rather than with the people running the business. Who controls those charitable holdings, how they vote, and whether they sell into the market on a schedule are questions not answered in the commitments themselves.
The Gates partnership runs over four years. The economic research fund will take time to produce findings. The founder pledges play out over a much longer horizon.
The documented commitments are concrete in dollar terms: $200 million here, $200 million there, $540 million in corporate contributions for 2025, and over $660 million in matching expenses across six months.

Investing in the public benefit
Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.
As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.
One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.
We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as a wholly-owned LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.
Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.
This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.
In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.
